clue.text: Get down to brass tacks giving speech to foreign country

blocks.note: talk is speech
a country abroad, seen from Britain

explanation.surface: A diplomat abroad stops waffling and makes a frank speech to the host nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are idioms for speaking frankly and dealing with the practical essentials of a matter.

clue.text: Creep like an amphibian?

blocks.note: first meaning: a sycophant, a flatterer
second meaning, playful: resembling a toad, the -Y suffix making an adjective

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the second meaning is a made-up adjective rather than a dictionary sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A fawning flatterer who sucks up to superiors is called a toady; a creep is the same kind of person.

clue.text: Coming from a hotel, ski very quickly

indicators.note: something coming from material is made out of it, so the letters are reworked into a new word

blocks.note: the letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A skier leaves the hotel and sets off downhill at speed.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means instantly or with great speed, like a bullet leaving a gun.

clue.text: Town will get burdens shifted

indicators.note: things shifted are moved about, so the letters are moved into a new order

blocks.note: the letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A town expects its heavy loads to be moved elsewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Tunbridge Wells is a spa town in Kent, proverbial in Britain for its conservative, letter-writing residents.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the name of a particular English town in Kent, so 'town' is its class.

clue.text: Deer — a thousand die before being reared

indicators.note: in a down entry, something reared is lifted upright, so the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: K is short for a thousand
a die is a cube
or is an old word for before, as in 'or ever'

explanation.surface: A deer dies before it is grown, a sad note from the hunting field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reared' looks like raising a young animal, but it means the pieces go upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A roebuck is the male of the roe, a small European species of deer.

clue.text: Half of them finished with improvement

definitions.note: a phrase standing for a past participle

indicators.note: half of a word is what is left once the other half is cut away

blocks.note: taken as written, then cut to its second half
finished means ended

explanation.surface: Half of the group stopped once things had got better.
explanation.definitionFit: A text that has been emended has been corrected, so it comes with improvement made.

clue.text: Double the ends over

indicators.note: turned over means flipped, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: tips are the ends of things

explanation.surface: An instruction to fold back both edges of a sheet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Double' looks like a verb about folding; it is a noun for a lookalike.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is the spit of another is their exact likeness, a double or twin.

clue.text: A superior poet

blocks.note: first meaning: the head of a religious house, ranking just below an abbot
second meaning: Matthew ..., English poet and diplomat of around 1700

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests praise of a fine poet; 'superior' is a noun, a monastic head.
explanation.definitionFit: A prior heads a priory, a monastic superior; Matthew Prior wrote light verse in the early eighteenth century.

clue.text: The month for lobster

blocks.note: first meaning: the eleventh month of the French Revolutionary calendar
second meaning: a rich creamy preparation in which lobster is served in its shell

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a seasonal tip on when lobster is best; one word is both a calendar month and a recipe name.
explanation.definitionFit: Thermidor was a summer month of the Revolutionary calendar, and lobster thermidor is a classic French dish named after a play.

clue.text: Cold that, in general, could become warmer

indicators.note: what could become something else is changed, so these letters are reworked

blocks.note: C stands for cold, as on a tap
the letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A general observation that cold weather can turn milder.
explanation.definitionFit: A home heating system is a device that warms rooms, so it is a warmer.

clue.text: Request put to an ecclesiastical organisation obliquely

blocks.note: to request is to ask
taken as written
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A petition is submitted to a church body in a roundabout way.
explanation.definitionFit: To look askance is to look sideways, with suspicion, so the word means at a slant.

clue.text: E's about to stop being solitary

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: two of the letter E
to remit is to cease or abate

explanation.surface: Someone called E is about to give up living alone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to stop' reads as 'on the point of stopping'; split it, and 'about' wraps the plural E's around a verb for stopping.
explanation.definitionFit: An eremite is a hermit, a religious recluse, and a solitary is the same kind of lone person.

clue.text: The old given a right to ring all the time

blocks.note: ye is an old spelling of the
taken as written
R is short for right
a ring is round in shape, and a round can be a circle

explanation.surface: An elderly person is granted the right to telephone whenever they like.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that happens throughout every season of the twelve months happens continually.

clue.text: In America connected many loose ends

blocks.note: an American spelling of through, as when a phone call is put through
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, so many

explanation.surface: In the States, many frayed threads were joined up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In America' applies to the first piece only, licensing the US spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrums are the unwoven tufts of warp thread left on a loom when the cloth is cut off.

clue.text: Hurt a child, a little boy

blocks.note: taken as written
CH is a standard abbreviation for child
a boy's name cut short, Edward made little

explanation.surface: Someone harmed a youngster, a small lad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hurt' looks like a transitive verb with a child as object; it is the definition, meaning felt pain.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are past-tense verbs for feeling pain, as a sore limb does.

clue.text: The surrounding numbers are level

blocks.note: surface reading: the figures arranged around something, as in a frame or border
setter's reading: every number is a perfect square, and a phrase built that way means even, as in a match

explanation.surface: Numbers on the border of a grid all come out even.
explanation.definitionFit: In a game or contest, the phrase means the scores are equal, with neither side ahead.

clue.text: Like Helen, got carried away

definitions.note: a phrase standing for an adjective

blocks.note: first meaning: Helen of Troy was abducted by Paris
second meaning: was taken off by force

explanation.walkthrough: 'Got carried away' suggests getting overexcited; here it is literal abduction.
explanation.definitionFit: Helen was seized and taken to Troy; to be seized and taken off against one's will is to be abducted.

clue.text: Procure a lot of seed and plant

indicators.note: a lot of something is most but not all of it, so one letter goes

blocks.note: to procure in the sense of supplying prostitutes
a kernel is the seed inside a nut or fruit stone

explanation.surface: Buy plenty of seed and sow it, a gardener's instruction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Procure' looks like plain buying; its job is the seamier sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The scarlet pimpernel is a small wild flower with red petals, so it is a plant.

clue.text: Environmental polluter gives dance a fresh start

indicators.note: a fresh start replaces the beginning, so the opening letter is changed

blocks.note: a lively swing dance of the 1940s

explanation.surface: A polluter revives an old dance, perhaps a dirty one.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the first letter of the dance for L, the learner's letter, to make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who drops rubbish in public places spoils the surroundings, a small-scale polluter.

clue.text: Enthusiast put up with cause of annoyance

blocks.note: a bug is a craze or an enthusiast, as in a camera bug
to put up with something is to bear it

explanation.surface: A keen fan tolerated something that irritated them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up with' is a single phrase in the surface, but 'with' is only the link.
explanation.definitionFit: A bugbear is a persistent source of irritation or dread, a pet hate.

clue.text: A wreath for Judy

definitions.note: a first name defining a surname

blocks.note: first meaning: a ring of flowers or leaves
second meaning: Judy ..., star of The Wizard of Oz

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like flowers bought for a woman; the second half is the actress's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A garland is a wreath of flowers, and Judy Garland was the Hollywood singer and actress.

clue.text: Pigeon with habitat beside river

blocks.note: an animal's habitat is its home
R is short for river

explanation.surface: A pigeon nesting on a riverbank.
explanation.definitionFit: A homing pigeon trained to fly back to its loft is called by this shorter name.

clue.text: Line from a man of letters, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is spoken aloud, so the sound matters, not the spelling

blocks.note: Q was the pen name of the writer Sir Arthur Quiller-Couch

explanation.surface: Quoting a sentence from a distinguished writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Line' suggests a line of verse; it is a line of people waiting.
explanation.definitionFit: A queue is a line of people waiting their turn, as at a bus stop.

clue.text: Some medicine — a sedative — gave relief

indicators.note: some of the words means only part of them, a run of letters inside

blocks.note: the run of letters spans the end of the first word and into the third

explanation.surface: A dose of a calming drug brought relief.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are past-tense verbs for lessening pain or discomfort.

clue.text: Vulgar slogan — “Bogeys all halved in birdies”

indicators.note: each word is cut in two and only its second half is kept

blocks.note: taken as written, then halved
taken as written, then halved
taken as written, then halved

explanation.surface: A golfer's crude motto about matching bogeys and birdies in a halved round.
explanation.walkthrough: Bogeys, birdies and halved holes are golf terms, all decoys; 'birdies' is the definition in its literal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The garganey is a small migratory dabbling duck, so the plural names a kind of bird.

clue.text: A Scotsman, St Andrew

blocks.note: S is short for saint
the familiar form of the name

explanation.surface: Saint Andrew, patron saint of Scotland, described as one of its own.
explanation.walkthrough: Sandy is a stock Scottish first name, short for Alexander, used for any Scotsman.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is so typical of Scotland that it serves as a generic nickname for a Scottish man.

clue.text: Jack got crack - that's clear

blocks.note: a jack, or jack tar, is a sailor, and AB is an able seaman
to crack a problem is to solve it

explanation.surface: A man named Jack has cracked the case, so everything is clear.
explanation.definitionFit: To absolve someone is to clear them of guilt or blame, as a court or a priest does.

clue.text: Go in van, touring the city

indicators.note: touring means travelling around, so the letters move about into a new order

blocks.note: the letters of these three words

explanation.surface: Take a van and drive around the town sightseeing.
explanation.definitionFit: Avignon is a city in Provence, in southern France, once the seat of the popes.

clue.text: The boy to move around

blocks.note: first meaning: a boy's name, short for Edward
second meaning: to swirl in a circular current

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a lad being told to shift about; the two halves are a name and a verb for swirling.
explanation.definitionFit: Water that eddies whirls in circles against the main current; Eddy is also a pet name for Edward.

clue.text: Extravagantly made up, pallid and gory

indicators.note: something made up is invented, so the letters are put together in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An actor in lavish horror make-up, pale and bloody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made up' suggests cosmetics; it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: The prodigal son wasted his inheritance, so to act prodigally is to spend lavishly and wastefully.
